transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-03-14
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes (recorder)
Attendees: Maya Chen - Redwood (AE), Tomas Rivera - Redwood (SE), Evan Brooks - Valerian (Head of Cloud Security), Priya Nair - Valerian (Platform Lead), Rafael Gomez - Valerian (Legal)
Recording link: https://redwood.example/s/meeting/ff-20280314-valerian (note: placeholder)

Auto-summary (generated):
- Customer evaluating options for Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments with strict EU residency + cross-border constraints for subset of data.
- Primary concerns: key residency, audit evidence for regulators, log retention & redaction, and latency impact for market data flows.
- Next steps: share architecture diagrams, run a pilot for private deployment timing, prepare a compliance pack.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you making time. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE. We also have Tomas on the call, our solutions engineer.
[00:06] Evan (Valerian): Hi, Evan here. Thanks. I know—I'll try to keep it short, we have a pretty specific ask around residency and evidence.
[00:12] Priya (Valerian): Priya on my side. We're the platform team owning the inference integration. Rafael from legal will jump in when needed.
[00:18] Rafael (Valerian): Hey all. Good to meet you.
[00:20] Tomas (Redwood): Quick agenda: 1) Gather constraints and success criteria; 2) map hosting options (hosted/dedicated/private); 3) go over keys/logs/retention; 4) next steps. Sound good?
[00:28] Evan: Yep. Goal: we need to know if you can keep EU personal data in-region for the whole lifecycle, including logs, and provide auditable evidence for our regulator. Also, some PII may also be considered heath-like data for research teams.
[00:38] Maya: Understood. When you say "whole lifecycle" can you clarify — ingestion, inference, logs, backups, and keystore?
[00:44] Evan: Exactly that. We need assurance that at-rest storage, keys, and audit trails for any redwood-handled telemetry can be pinned to EU.
[00:51] Tomas: Quick note, we have region-locking for Private and for Dedicated in certain regions; Hosted can be region pinned in our EU cluster but there are caveats around shared control plane artifacts.
[01:00] Priya: Caveats meaning — what artifacts are potentially outside region?
[01:03] Tomas: The control plane metadata such as billing events, aggregated usage metrics, and some multi-tenant analytics are in our control plane which today is hosted in multiple regions. For our Private offering the control plane sits inside your VPC if desired. For Dedicated, we can offer an isolated tenant with logging routed to your SIEM.
[01:18] Rafael: From legal: we need a written map of data flows, statement of residency for keys, and proof of SOC2 or equivalent for the environment storing logs. Is that something you can provide?
[01:26] Maya: Yes, we can provide SOC2 reports, ISO artifacts, and a dataflow diagram. We'll attach the compliance pack. Note: some artifacts are redacted but can be provided under NDA — we'll flag that in the pack.
[01:34] Evan: Also key management. Our policy says our master key must not leave the EU and must be under our KMS or an HSM. Can Redwood integrate with an external KMS/HSM and allow customer-controlled keys?
[01:45] Tomas: Yes — Private allows customer-managed keys and HSM. For Dedicated we support bring-your-own-key with KMS integrations and key escrow options. For Hosted, we do offer customer KMS integrations in EU regions but there are tokenization and cache considerations — specifically the runtime uses an ephemeral local key for session cache that is not the customer master key.
[02:02] Priya: When you say ephemeral local key — is that ephemeral in-memory only or written to disk? Our auditors don't like anything persistent outside the region.
[02:09] Tomas: It's in-memory only and we can configure vault mount points so no disk writes occur. I should caveat, older runtime versions had a small local cache spill scenario, but current builds have mitigations. We'll include the kernel-level notes.
[02:20] Maya: Noted. Evan, what are your regulator's expected retention windows for logs? 
[02:25] Evan: For auth logs and audit trails it's seven years for certain datasets; for general telemetry maybe 1-2 years. Also we need eDiscovery capability for legal holds.
[02:36] Rafael: On that point, we need a process: when a legal hold is issued we must capture relevant inference inputs and outputs and ensure they cannot be discarded — subject to redaction where required.
[02:47] Tomas: We support retention policies per-route/model. For Private and Dedicated you can set retention and hook your archival system (S3 in-region). For Hosted we provide configurable retention but long-term archival into customer-owned buckets is the recommended pattern.
[02:59] Priya: Does Redwood's Hosted offering ever store logs outside the region for redundancy?
[03:04] Tomas: Not as a default for EU region accounts; however cross-region failover could replicate metadata for availability. We can set strict region affinity and disable cross-region replication for accounts under enterprise contracts.
[03:15] Evan: Ok. Another question: how do you handle redaction of sensitive fields in logs? We need automatic PII scrubbing and ability to whitelist fields for capture.
[03:24] Tomas: We offer configurable redaction rules and we also support pre-ingest tokenization. The redaction engine runs prior to logging to our control plane. In Private deployments you can run the redaction appliance inside your network.
[03:35] Rafael: Will you provide a sketch of the redaction pipeline? Our compliance folks will want to know where scrubbing runs and proof points that scrubbed data can't be rehydrated.
[03:43] Maya: We'll include a diagram and the scrub guarantees. We'll also share the cryptographic proof approach we use for irreversible hashing.
[03:50] Evan: Performance worry: if we enable aggressive redaction and in-region KMS calls per token, what's the latency hit? For trading systems we need sub-150ms tail for small queries.
[03:59] Tomas: Good point. In Private/deployed-on-prem we can often meet sub-100ms since keys are local and there's no cross-region RTT. For Dedicated, with regional colocations, typical tails are ~120-160ms depending on sequence length and batching. Hosted with cross-tenant caches might see higher—again, dependent on workload. We'll produce a sample run for your payload.
[04:20] Priya: Can you quantify the difference in cost or ops overhead between Dedicated and Private for us?
[04:24] Maya: High-level: Private usually has higher one-time setup and ongoing infra ops, Dedicated has recurring reserved capacity but less ops for you, Hosted is cheapest but with least control. Tomas will put numbers against your sampled traffic.
[04:34] Evan: Another pain point: audit evidence during an inspection. When a regulator requests a snapshot, can Redwood produce a tamper-evident export of logs and key access events?
[04:44] Tomas: We support signed log exports and sequencing. For Private we can also run an attestation agent that signs exported bundles with your key. For Hosted, we provide signed artifacts but the signing root is Redwood unless you supply an attestation key via BYOK flow.
[04:58] Rafael: On BYOK, what's the escrow story? We have legal constraints about key escrow and must know who can access the key, under what court orders, etc.
[05:07] Maya: We have documented key escrow policies. Briefly: for Dedicated/Private customer keys remain under customer control; Redwood will not escrow keys unless agreed contractually and under strict access controls with court-order process that we document. We'll include the legal matrix.
[05:20] Evan: Good. Data residency nuance: some analytic derivatives from models (e.g., embeddings) may be considered personal data; we need to ensure derivative data is handled accordingly.
[05:29] Tomas: We classify derivative artifacts by route. You can opt out of persistent embedding storage, or set it to in-region only and TTL it. We'll show the config options.
[05:38] Priya: Is there an option to disable telemetry entirely for specific models/routes?
[05:41] Tomas: Yes — telemetry can be disabled at route-level in Dedicated and Private. Hosted has limited opt-out for platform metrics but we can discuss contract level exceptions.
[05:51] Maya: Rafael, any legal questions at this stage aside from key escrow and evidence?
[05:56] Rafael: Data transfer mechanisms. If you rely on standard contractual clauses (SCCs) or EU-US DPF stuff, we need to map which artifacts are covered. Also where backups land, and whether Redwood subprocessors are in scope.
[06:07] Tomas: Redwood's subprocessors list is in our security pack; most hosting providers and observability vendors are subprocessors. For Private deployments you control subprocessors. For Dedicated we minimize third-party dependencies and can provide a subprocessors roster for review.
[06:20] Evan: Ok, let's drill into an example flow. We have a customer-facing assistant that takes name, account ID, and a short message, then calls an inference endpoint. We want to keep the account ID immutable inside EU and ensure that any logs redact the ID. Walk us through the options.
[06:35] Tomas: Option A: Hosted with tokenization at client side; tokens stored in-region and logs only show tokenized ID. Option B: Dedicated with in-region keys and redaction at ingress. Option C: Private where the whole stack is inside your VPC and logs never leave your bucket.
[06:49] Priya: If we do Hosted + tokenization, are there edge cases where the plaintext ID could appear in a model's output? We need to avoid leakage into outputs that might be retained in cache.
[06:58] Tomas: Model outputs can be configured not to be cached. We have config to prevent outputs from being written to any persistent store. For Hosted, you must enable those flags; for Dedicated/Private we can default to non-persistent outputs per your policy.
[07:11] Evan: Great. About caches — what's the KV cache behavior and where does it live?
[07:15] Tomas: The KV cache is held in memory in the serving runtime. For long-running sessions we maintain it per-instance. There's an optional encrypted disk spill to local ephemeral volumes in some configs; we can disable spill for your deployment.
[07:26] Priya: You mentioned older runtime versions had a small cache spill — can you give us a CVE or ticket reference so we can validate it's fixed?
[07:33] Tomas: I'll include the ticket and the runtime release notes.
[07:36] Rafael: Regarding incident response: if there's suspected exfiltration, can Redwood provide a timeline of events and a signed export of accesses to keys and logs?
[07:45] Tomas: Yes, we have an IR playbook. Private and Dedicated allow full forensic exports. Hosted allows exports but there are rate limitations; for urgent forensics we do support expedited exports under enterprise SLA.
[07:58] Maya: Quick check — what's your timeline for a procurement/legal review and a pilot?
[08:03] Evan: We'd like to get legal sign-off within 6 weeks and pilot within 10-12 weeks if the architecture looks good. Procurement needs SOC2 + subprocessors list and a redacted runbook.
[08:12] Maya: We'll aim to get the compliance pack and runbooks to you by Friday (2028-03-17).
[08:18] Rafael: On evidence, is there an automated way to demonstrate encryption-in-use and access authorization logs that we can hand to auditors?
[08:25] Tomas: We provide time-stamped access logs and signed artifacts. We can also run short attestation checks during audits and produce signed statements of recent configuration.
[08:34] Evan: Network egress controls — can we restrict outbound connections from inference hosts to only our approved endpoints?
[08:39] Tomas: In Private yes. For Dedicated, we can do network policies that restrict egress. Hosted is more rigid but we do have egress allowlisting for enterprise agreements.
[08:50] Priya: A question about backups — do you snapshot model weights? And if so, where are snapshots stored?
[08:56] Tomas: We snapshot model artifacts for faster deployment and rollback. For Private, snapshots are in your storage; for Dedicated we store them in your dedicated tenant storage region. Hosted snapshots for curated models live in Redwood-managed buckets but we can provide attestations and retention settings.
[09:13] Evan: If we want to run an initial pilot, we're leaning Private for one business unit and Dedicated for lower-risk flows. What's the setup timeline?
[09:22] Maya: Private on-prem can be a multi-month engagement depending on hardware procurement. We have a "fast private" program that deploys into customer cloud VPCs in 4-6 weeks if infra is ready. Dedicated typically 2-4 weeks once seats and capacity are agreed.
[09:36] Priya: Cost roughly?
[09:39] Maya: Tomas will share a sample estimate. High level: Dedicated = reserved monthly; Private = upfront infra + license. We'll email specifics.
[09:46] Tomas: I'll prepare a cost matrix for the sample workload and we'll include latency numbers.
[09:52] Evan: One more regulatory nuance: our regulator asks for proof that PII is not used to retrain models without consent. How do you attest to training data usage?
[10:02] Tomas: We have a policy that customer data is not used for model training unless explicitly opted-in; we can include contract language and provide logs showing training pipeline inputs. For Hosted, training isolation is documented.
[10:15] Rafael: If we sign, will Redwood accept contract clauses for residency and audit rights?
[10:20] Maya: We have enterprise contract addenda for residency and audit. We'll surface the standard language and then legal can triage modifications.
[10:28] Evan: Ok, let's capture concrete deliverables — please confirm what you'll send this week.
[10:33] Maya: Compliance pack (SOC2, ISO, subprocessors), redaction pipeline diagram, BYOK and key escrow policy, sample latency/cost matrix for your traffic, and a proposed pilot plan.
[10:44] Rafael: We also need the subprocessors list and a draft data processing addendum.
[10:48] Maya: Yes — will include.
[10:50] Priya: For the pilot, we'll want an SE workshop to design the benchmark. Can Tomas run that?
[10:55] Tomas: Absolutely, I'll do a 2-hour workshop and then a runbook to execute the benchmark.
[11:00] Evan: Thanks everyone — this was useful.
[11:03] Maya: Thanks — we'll follow up with the pack and schedule the SE workshop.
[11:08] Rafael: We'll review and come back with redlines.
[11:11] Tomas: I'll include the kernel notes and ticket refs for the runtime fixes.
[11:15] Maya: Great. End of recording.
